messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
A metric space (M,d) is complete exactly when every Cauchy sequence in M converges to a point of M.
What does the nested diameter condition imply?
The sequence (F_n) consists of nonempty closed subsets with F_{n+1} \subset F_n and with the diameter of F_n tending to 0 as n \rightarrow \infty.
One can choose points x_n in F_n, and then the nested diameter condition makes x_n Cauchy because d(x_n,x_m) \le \operatorname{diam}(F_n) for all m \ge n.
Completeness gives a limit x of x_n in M, and the nested closedness forces x to lie in every F_k because the subsequence from k on stays in F_k and converges to x, so the intersection is nonempty.
What does the reverse direction show?
For a Cauchy sequence (x_n), the sets F_n = closure of {x_k : k \ge n} are nonempty closed, nested, and their diameters tend to 0 because the Cauchy tails have arbitrarily small diameter.
Does the intersection then yield completeness?
By the assumed property, the intersection contains a point x, and since x is in the closure of every tail, the Cauchy property forces d(x,x_n) to tend to 0, so M is complete.

A metric space (M,d) is complete exactly when every Cauchy sequence in M converges to a point of M.
What does the nested diameter condition imply?
The sequence (F_n) consists of nonempty closed subsets with F_{n+1} \subset F_n and with the diameter of F_n tending to 0 as n \rightarrow \infty.
One can choose points x_n in F_n, and then the nested diameter condition makes x_n Cauchy because d(x_n,x_m) \le \operatorname{diam}(F_n) for all m \ge n.
Completeness gives a limit x of x_n in M, and the nested closedness forces x to lie in every F_k because the subsequence from k on stays in F_k and converges to x, so the intersection is nonempty.
What does the reverse direction show?
For a Cauchy sequence (x_n), the sets F_n = closure of {x_k : k \ge n} are nonempty closed, nested, and their diameters tend to 0 because the Cauchy tails have arbitrarily small diameter.
Does the intersection then yield completeness?
By the assumed property, the intersection contains a point x, and for every tail the Cauchy distance estimates plus membership of x in its closure force x_n to converge to x, so M is complete.
